Cook to the cited temperature threshold rather than to the clock alone.
summary: A bone-in lamb shoulder studded with garlic and rosemary, roasted covered over onion, garlic and water for 3 hours, then uncovered in a hotter oven to brown. The long, covered, moist cooking softens the meat enough to pull it off the bone. Cook until fork-tender, even if it has already lost its pink colour; any leftovers depend on portion sizes.

ingredients.note: See the yield note for smaller, boneless and rolled shoulders.

ingredients.quantity: 1 cup, plus ¾ cup more if the pan runs dry

method.instruction: Heat the oven to 240°C conventional, or 220°C fan-forced. Both figures are the source's. The source names no shelf; a middle shelf is this project's ordinary default, not a source instruction.
Rub the lamb with the oil, salt and pepper. With a thin, sharp knife make 12 deep cuts in it, without going through to the underside, and push rosemary and garlic slivers into each one.

Put the onion, the halved garlic head and the remaining rosemary in the bottom of a roasting pan, sit the lamb on top and pour the water around it. The source gives no pan size; one the shoulder fits in with a little room is enough.
Cover with a lid or tightly with a double layer of foil. Put it in the oven and turn the oven down straight away to 180°C conventional, or 160°C fan-forced. Roast, covered, for 3 hours.

Take off the foil and check there is still liquid in the pan; if not, add ¾ cup water. Turn the oven up to 220°C and roast for 20 to 30 minutes more, until the outside is brown and crisp. The source gives no fan figure for this last stage, and none is converted here.

Test whether the meat parts easily with two forks. If not, follow the source's recovery: cover again and return to 180°C conventional or 160°C fan-forced until tender, then check again. Tenderness is not a temperature measurement: probe the thickest part away from bone. Health Canada gives 77°C internal for well-done whole lamb cuts; FSANZ recommends at least 75°C for rolled roasts. Check the applicable endpoint rather than assuming tenderness proves it.

Transfer the lamb to a plate, cover loosely with foil and rest for 20 minutes, then pull the meat off the bone with tongs and serve, or promptly portion and chill it. The source allows a longer rest, up to a couple of hours; that is not blanket permission to leave it on the bench. Any extended wait needs controlled hot holding or prompt chilling under applicable local storage guidance, not just foil and towels.

yield_note: The source's recipe card gives 4 servings, and its notes say a 1.5 kg shoulder gives about 700 g of cooked meat, which feeds about 4. Source times: 15 minutes preparation and 3 hours 30 minutes cooking, plus resting. The source's adjustments: for a smaller shoulder of around 1 kg, or a boneless one, cut the covered time by 20 minutes; a 1.8 kg bone-in shoulder weighs about 1.3 kg boned; a rolled boneless shoulder of about 1.1 to 1.3 kg takes the recipe's time as written; two shoulders of about 1.5 kg each fit in one pan with 30 minutes added to the covered time. The source also gives a pan gravy, which is left out of this record.

provenance_note: Recipe facts paraphrased from Nagi Maehashi's page at RecipeTin Eats, accessed 2026-10-06; the safety and leftovers figures are Health Canada's and FSANZ's, from the same date. The recipe source checks whether the meat separates easily with a fork. Also check the centre temperature with a thermometer; tenderness alone cannot establish the safety endpoint. Its first and second oven settings come with fan figures; its final 220°C browning stage does not, and that is recorded as written. The source gives no storage, cooling or reheating advice; all of that in this record comes from the food-safety guides and is credited to them. The source recommends covering and cooking further if the shoulder is still tough. This version uses an initial 20 minutes of rest before serving or prompt chilling. A longer wait requires controlled hot holding or storage; do not leave it on the bench.

caveats: Shopping names: lamb shoulder (羊肩肉), bone in, is the cut this source is written for. Boneless and rolled boneless shoulders are also sold; the source's time adjustments for them are in the yield note. A rolled roast falls under FSANZ's at-least-75°C recommendation.

Cooling: a big piece of hot meat cools slowly. FSANZ advises cooling cooked food quickly, for example in shallow containers in the fridge. Pulling the meat off the bone and spreading it out in shallow containers before chilling is one way to do that. Pour the pan juices into a separate container; the fat sets on top in the fridge and lifts off.

Storage: use the FSANZ cumulative 2-hour/4-hour rule for potentially hazardous food between 5°C and 60°C, counting preparation, transport and serving together: under 2 hours, use or refrigerate; from 2 to less than 4 hours, use immediately, do not refrigerate again; 4 hours or more, discard. Keep chilled food at 5°C or colder and use within a few days. Resting is not an exemption from these controls.
Reheating: FSANZ says to reheat cold food quickly to piping hot; Health Canada's figure for leftovers is 74°C in the centre. A splash of the reserved juices stops pulled meat drying out.
Hot fat and steam: the pan holds hot liquid and fat after 3 hours. Lift the foil away from you and move the pan with both hands.
